turns.content: Hi! I'm working on a project about food security in Mexico and would love to start by getting some basic data on the topic. Could you help me with that?

Here are some core, recent facts you can use as a starting point for food security in Mexico (using latest available FAO data, which are 3‑year averages):

**Data:**

1. **How many people are food insecure?**

- People who are **moderately or severely food insecure** (3‑year average 2022–2024, labeled 2024):  
  - About <claim id="5a2421dc" policy="auto">25.1</claim> million people.  
  - 90% confidence interval: from <claim id="d101a123" policy="auto">24.3</claim> to <claim id="9afb01cc" policy="auto">25.9</claim> million.

- People who are **severely food insecure** (3‑year average 2022–2024, labeled 2024):  
  - About <claim id="5c6c60e8" policy="auto">3.8</claim> million people.  
  - 90% confidence interval: from <claim id="f8cda67f" policy="auto">3.5</claim> to <claim id="df4b4261" policy="auto">4.1</claim> million.

(“Moderate or severe” includes households with compromised diet quality and/or quantity; “severe” reflects very serious experiences like going a whole day without eating due to lack of resources.)

2. **What share of the population is food insecure?**

- **Prevalence of moderate or severe food insecurity** in the total population (3‑year average 2022–2024, labeled 2024):  
  - <claim id="2bf31719" policy="auto">19.3</claim>% of the population.  
  - 90% confidence interval: from <claim id="8484c310" policy="auto">18.7</claim>% to <claim id="bbb072f0" policy="auto">20</claim>%.

- **Prevalence of severe food insecurity** in the total population (3‑year average 2022–2024, labeled 2024):  
  - <claim id="555f34c7" policy="auto">2.9</claim>% of the population.  
  - 90% confidence interval: from <claim id="bdb21340" policy="auto">2.7</claim>% to <claim id="3aee3abf" policy="auto">3.1</claim>%.

3. **Recent trend (approximate, using 3‑year averages)**

- Moderate or severe food insecurity prevalence (% of population):  
  - 2019 (2017–2019): <claim id="03692bdf" policy="auto">23.8</claim>%  
  - 2020 (2018–2020): <claim id="72132f39" policy="auto">25.3</claim>%  
  - 2021 (2019–2021): <claim id="2a987873" policy="auto">25.5</claim>%  
  - 2022 (2020–2022): <claim id="619c57e7" policy="auto">23.5</claim>%  
  - 2023 (2021–2023): <claim id="df9f1609" policy="auto">20.7</claim>%  
  - 2024 (2022–2024): <claim id="2bf31719" policy="auto">19.3</claim>%

- Severe food insecurity prevalence (% of population):  
  - 2019 (2017–2019): <claim id="6f0f4c39" policy="auto">3.8</claim>%  
  - 2020 (2018–2020): <claim id="40e59813" policy="auto">3.8</claim>%  
  - 2021 (2019–2021): <claim id="917f5308" policy="auto">3.5</claim>%  
  - 2022 (2020–2022): <claim id="04ecaf0d" policy="auto">3.2</claim>%  
  - 2023 (2021–2023): <claim id="d0c94917" policy="auto">3</claim>%  
  - 2024 (2022–2024): <claim id="555f34c7" policy="auto">2.9</claim>%

**Analysis (very concise):**

- Around **one in five people in Mexico** experienced **moderate or severe food insecurity** in the 2022–2024 period, and just under **3% experienced severe food insecurity**.
- Both **moderate+severe** and **severe** food insecurity **rose around 2019–2021** (capturing the COVID‑19 period) and have **declined since**, but remain higher than ideal for an upper‑middle‑income country.
- In absolute terms, roughly **25 million people** are affected by moderate or severe food insecurity, and nearly **4 million** by severe food insecurity, underscoring the scale of the challenge even as recent trends show some improvement.

**Note on interpretation:**

- These are **3‑year moving averages**, so “2024” actually summarizes 2022–2024 and smooths short‑term shocks.
- Indicators are based on the **Food Insecurity Experience Scale (FIES)**, capturing people’s *experiences* of constrained access to food, not just calorie availability or poverty.

**Sources:**

- **FAO — Suite of Food Security Indicators (FAO_FS)**  
  - *Prevalence of moderate or severe food insecurity in the total population (percent) (3-year average)* — indicator FAO_FS_210091 (SDG 2.1.2).  
  - *Prevalence of severe food insecurity in the total population (percent) (3-year average)* — indicator FAO_FS_210401.  
  - *Moderately or severely food insecure people (million) (3-year average)* — indicator FAO_FS_210081.  
  - *Severely food insecure people (million) (3-year average)* — indicator FAO_FS_210071.  

**Suggested follow-ups:**

1. Could you show this Mexico food insecurity trend in a simple chart that I can use in a presentation?  
2. Can you compare Mexico’s food insecurity levels to those of another country or to the Latin America & Caribbean average?  
3. Can you help me connect these food insecurity numbers to poverty or income inequality data for Mexico?

indicator_metadata.name: Prevalence of moderate or severe food insecurity in the total population (percent) (3-year average)
indicator_metadata.measurement_unit: Percentage, Upper Bound for the 90% confidence interval, Lower Bound for the 90% confidence interval
indicator_metadata.definition_long:
The prevalence of moderate or severe food insecurity is an estimate of the percentage of people in the population who live in households classified as moderately or severely food insecure.
The assessment is conducted using data collected with the Food Insecurity Experience Scale or a compatible experience-based food security measurement questionnaire (such as the HFSSM).
The probability to be food insecure is estimated using the one-parameter logistic Item Response Theory model (the Rasch model) and thresholds for classification are made cross country comparable by calibrating the metrics obtained in each country against the FIES global reference scale, maintained by FAO. The threshold to classify "moderate or severe" food insecurity corresponds to the severity associated with the item "having to eat less" on the global FIES scale.
In simpler terms, a household is classified as moderately or severely food insecure when at least one adult in the household has reported to have been exposed, at times during the year, to low quality diets and might have been forced to also reduce the quantity of food they would normally eat because of a lack of money or other resources. 
It is an indicator of lack of food access.
Confidence intervals at 90% level are also available. They are computed considering both sampling and measurement variability.
indicator_metadata.methodology:
See the linked spreadsheet. 

More details on the methodology for computing the prevalence of severe food insecurity are in "Methods for estimating comparable prevalence rates of food insecurity experienced by adults throughout the world", Voices of the Hungry Technical Report N. 1, April 2016 (http://www.fao.org/3/c-i4830e.pdf ).
See also the metadata document at https://unstats.un.org/sdgs/metadata/files/Metadata-02-02-01.pdf.
indicator_metadata.relevance: This is indicator 2.1.2 in the SDG framework, to monitor target 2.1 ("By 2030, end hunger and ensure access by all people, […], to safe, nutritious and sufficient food all year round").
indicator_metadata.aggregation_method: The aggregates are computed using a weighted population average.
indicator_metadata.confidentiality: This work is made available under the Creative Commons Attribution-NonCommercial-ShareAlike 3.0 IGO license (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-nc-sa/3.0/igo/). In addition to this license, some database specific terms of use are listed: Terms of Use of Datasets (https://www.fao.org/contact-us/terms/db-terms-of-use/en/).

indicator_metadata.measurement_unit: Percentage, Upper Bound for the 90% confidence interval, Lower Bound for the 90% confidence interval
indicator_metadata.definition_long:
The prevalence of severe food insecurity is an estimate of the percentage of people in the population who live in households classified as severely food insecure.
The assessment is conducted using data collected with the Food Insecurity Experience Scale or a compatible experience-based food security measurement questionnaire (such as the HFSSM).
The probability to be food insecure is estimated using the one-parameter logistic Item Response Theory model (the Rasch model) and thresholds for classification are made cross country comparable by calibrating the metrics obtained in each country against the FIES global reference scale, maintained by FAO. The threshold to classify "severe" food insecurity corresponds to the severity associated with the item "having not eaten for an entire day" on the global FIES scale.
In simpler terms, a household is classified as severely food insecure when at least one adult in the household has reported to have been exposed, at times during the year, to several of the most severe experiences described in the FIES questions, such as to have been forced to reduce the quantity of the food, to have skipped meals, having gone hungry, or having to go for a whole day without eating because of a lack of money or other resources. 
It is an indicator of lack of food access.
Confidence intervals at 90% level are also available. They are computed considering both sampling and measurement variability.
indicator_metadata.methodology:
More details on the methodology for computing the prevalence of severe food insecurity are in "Methods for estimating comparable prevalence rates of food insecurity experienced by adults throughout the world", Voices of the Hungry Technical Report N. 1, April 2016 (http://www.fao.org/3/c-i4830e.pdf ).
See also the metadata document at https://unstats.un.org/sdgs/metadata/files/Metadata-02-02-01.pdf.
